name: Braulio of Zaragoza
knownFor: Bishop of Zaragoza in Visigothic Spain, friend and editor of Isidore of Seville, and a letter writer. He wrote to Pope Honorius for the bishops of Spain in 638.
dates: Bishop of Zaragoza for about twenty years, under Kings Sisenand, Chintila, Tulga and Chindaswinth, Ildefonsus of Toledo says. He signed the fourth, fifth and sixth councils of Toledo. The acts date the fourth and sixth to the Spanish eras 671 and 676, which are 633 and 638. No held source gives his birth or the year of his death
place: Zaragoza, where he followed his brother John as bishop; the councils at Toledo

keyWorks.title: Letters
keyWorks.about: among them letters to Isidore of Seville, to Kings Chindaswinth and Reccesvinth, and to the priest Taio. One, to Pope Honorius, he wrote for the bishops of Spain

keyWorks.title: Life of Saint Aemilian
keyWorks.about: the Life of a monk named Aemilian, sent to his brother Fronimian, a priest. Ildefonsus of Toledo says it keeps Braulio's own memory and makes the holy man's virtue known

keyWorks.title: List of Isidore's works
keyWorks.about: his notice of Isidore of Seville and his books. In it he says he divided the Etymologies into twenty books, since Isidore wrote it at his request

traces: Isidore of Seville sent him the Etymologies, which Braulio says Isidore wrote at his request. Braulio divided the work into twenty books.
Ildefonsus of Toledo gives him a chapter in his book of famous church writers.
Ildefonsus's book tells of a Toledo cleric named Eugenius who became a monk at Zaragoza and then bishop of Toledo, Eugenius the second. He may be the archdeacon Braulio gave up to King Chindaswinth.
remembered: Nicolás Antonio, in his Bibliotheca Hispana vetus, quotes a chronicle he gives to Isidore, bishop of Pax. Theodor Mommsen, who edits it, says it runs to 754 and calls the name false.
The chronicle says Braulio shone at a council of Toledo under King Sisenand, which Mommsen identifies as the fourth. Rome later marveled at his eloquence through a letter, it adds.
At a later council under King Chintila, which Antonio takes as the sixth, the chronicle says he poured devout teaching into Christian minds. It adds that the church still read his short works.

uncertain: His life is known from his own letters, from Ildefonsus's short chapter on him and from the acts of the councils he signed.

Whether his archdeacon Eugenius is the Eugenius whom Ildefonsus makes bishop of Toledo. Braulio's letters and the king's do not name the city. Ildefonsus tells of a Toledo cleric named Eugenius who became a monk at Zaragoza and was brought back by the king's force. The match rests on these two accounts.

Whom Pope Honorius meant by the faithless. Braulio's reply speaks of the faithless. It also denies a rumor that a ruling of the Roman prince let baptized Jews return to what it calls their superstition. The pope's letter is not held.

His age and death. His letter to the king speaks of his age and his failing sight. No held source gives the year of his death. Theodor Mommsen, from Ildefonsus's list of kings, puts it under Chindaswinth, between 641 and 652. His name is missing from the acts of the seventh council of Toledo, Antonio notes, and by the eighth, Taio was bishop of Zaragoza.

Whether Braulio wrote the notice of Isidore's works. A note printed with Nicolás Antonio's notice says Gregorius Mayansius denied it. The note keeps it as his, as all the old manuscripts its writer had seen and nearly all bibliographers agree.
